title: Countries added 333 new trade barriers in six months, says the WTO
subtitle: A new WTO report shows rules that block trade are piling up, but steps that make trade easier grew even faster.
content_html:
Picture this. Between January and June 2026, governments around the world brought in 333 new rules that make trade harder. That is more than the 300 such rules they added in the whole of 2025. The World Trade Organization (WTO) shared these numbers in a report on Tuesday, 17 November 2026.

But there is a twist. In the same six months, countries also brought in 466 rules that make trade easier, up from 391 in all of 2025. So the world is building walls and opening gates at the same time. For an Indian exporter, both matter.

What is the WTO, in one minute?

The WTO is a global body based in Geneva, Switzerland. It started on 1 January 1995 and has 166 members. Think of it as the umpire of world trade. Its members agree on the rules, and the WTO keeps a close eye on what each member does.

Since 2009, the WTO chief has put out regular reports that count these trade steps. The new one covers rules brought in up to 30 June 2026.

Walls and gates: what do these words mean?

A trade restriction is anything that makes it harder or costlier to buy from or sell to another country. A tariff is the best known one. It is a tax on goods coming in. Picture a samosa stall that must pay Rs 2 more on every packet of imported spice. The stall either earns less or charges you more. Bans and export controls (rules that stop some goods from leaving a country) are other kinds.

A trade-facilitating step works the other way. It makes trade cheaper or quicker. A tariff cut, a lower tax on goods going out, or faster customs checks at a port all count. This is like a toll booth that suddenly lets cars through for free.

How big are the walls?

The 333 new restrictions in the first half of 2026 touched imports worth $2 trillion, or 8% of everything the world buys from abroad. On the selling side, new export rules covered $794 billion, or 3.2% of world exports.

Rules also pile up. A tariff added years ago may still be in force today. The WTO adds up all such import rules brought in since 2009 that are still alive. By 30 June 2026, they covered $5.4 trillion of trade, or 21.3% of world imports. That is roughly one in every five dollars the world spends on imports, and the highest level since the WTO began this count in 2009.

WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala said "the stockpile of trade-restrictive measures continues to grow".

And how big are the gates?

The easing side grew faster. New rules that make imports easier covered $1.3 trillion, or 5.2% of world imports. New support for exporters, like cuts in export taxes, reached a record $570 billion, or 2.3% of world exports. In all of 2025, that figure was just $102 billion. So it jumped more than five times in half a year.

Why? The WTO says much of the rise came from short-term steps taken after trade through the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted. When a key sea route gets blocked, countries rush to cut taxes and speed up paperwork so goods keep moving, like a school opening an extra gate when the main one is jammed.

The WTO also said that in most sectors it looked at, new easing rules covered a bigger share of imports than new blocking rules. The only exceptions were electric vehicles and solar cells, where big economies are fighting hard for market share.

Is world trade shrinking then?

No. The WTO says goods trade held up better than expected in the first half of 2026, helped a lot by strong demand for goods that power artificial intelligence. It raised its forecast for growth in world goods trade this year to 3.9%, up from 1.9% in March.

What does this mean for Indian exporters?

The WTO's news release gives world totals and does not single out any one country. But the walls are real for Indian sellers. Just a day before the report, on Monday 16 November, the European Union put a 9.5% anti-dumping duty on some cold-rolled steel from India. An anti-dumping duty is an extra tax a country charges when it finds goods are being sold to it below a fair price. India sold 282 million euros of this steel to the EU, as per the European Commission.

Such cases keep coming. The WTO counted 218 new trade remedy probes (checks into whether imports are unfairly cheap or rising too fast) in the first half of 2026. That is 36.3 a month, against 32.6 a month in 2025. Anti-dumping duties remained the most used tool.

The gates matter just as much. When a country cuts the tax on goods coming in, an Indian shirt sent there gets cheaper for the buyer. That can help an Indian seller win the order.

The simple takeaway

Think of world trade like a cricket ground with many entry gates. In the first six months of 2026, countries locked 333 gates and opened 466. The locked ones, built up since 2009, now cover about a fifth of world imports, a record. For anyone planning to sell abroad one day, the lesson is simple: check the tariff and customs rules of the buyer's country before you set your price.
